canonical_topic: Why power markets run two auctions (day-ahead and real-time)
definition: Two sequential auctions exist because generation fleets can't ramp instantly: the day-ahead market commits plants in half-hour or hourly blocks based on expected load, and the real-time market covers any load that shows up between those commitment intervals.
core_idea: Day-ahead scheduling activates generators in discrete time blocks sized to the load expected at the start of each block; any demand that materializes before the next block's units come online has to be served by real-time, which is why real-time prices react to short-term swings in hourly demand.
key_points: Day-ahead activates generation in half-hour or hour-long increments, sized to load at the start of the period.
Demand increases occurring before the next scheduled activation must be met by the real-time market.
This structural lag is the mechanical reason real-time prices move with short-term demand changes.
relationships: Feeds into why the real-time and day-ahead generation stacks end up similar (see companion item on stack overlap).
trading_implications: Short-term demand ramps that outrun the day-ahead commitment schedule are a structural driver of real-time price spikes, independent of any generation shortage.
caveats: Real-time price volatility is not necessarily a sign of a supply shortfall; it can simply reflect the lag between demand realization and the next scheduled unit commitment.
